1989 · WWW

What if every idea could connect?

March 1989: proposal. By the end of 1990: the first browser and server.

One link. A world of possibilities.

At CERN, information lived across different computers, formats and teams. Tim Berners-Lee proposed a way to connect it: a web of documents anyone could follow.

The Internet already connected computers. The Web added a shared way to identify, retrieve and link information. Robert Cailliau helped develop and champion the project; Nicola Pellow built a browser that could run on many kinds of computer. A working Web was a collaborative achievement.

Tim Berners-Lee — CERN · Original proposal

1990 · HTML

A page. An address. A way to get there.

1990: first implementation. 1991: the Web is announced more widely.

HTML + URL + HTTP

HTML gives a document structure and links. A URL identifies a resource. HTTP lets a browser request it. Together, they turn scattered files into a navigable Web.

HTML describes what content is: a heading, a paragraph or a link. It is markup, not a programming language. In 1993, NCSA Mosaic, developed by a team including Marc Andreessen and Eric Bina, helped bring the graphical Web to a much wider audience. The small example here uses modern HTML syntax to demonstrate the original idea.

1993–94 · CGI / Cookie

Now the page can remember you.

1993: CGI in use. 1994: Netscape introduces cookies.

From publishing to participating.

Forms and CGI let a request trigger a program on a server. Cookies add a small piece of browser-held state. A website can accept an order, recognize a returning visitor and keep a session going.

HTTP requests do not automatically remember earlier ones. A server can send a session identifier in a cookie, then look up the matching cart on later requests. The cookie is often an identifier, not the whole cart. CGI is an interface between a web server and a program; later systems such as PHP and application servers make this pattern easier to build.

1994 · CSS

Same content. A different world.

1994: Lie proposes CSS. December 1996: CSS1 becomes a W3C Recommendation.

Structure gets a sense of style.

HTML alone cannot express every design decision. CSS separates presentation from content: one set of rules can change typography, spacing, color and layout across a whole website.

The cascade gives rules from different sources a defined way to work together. Inheritance lets some properties pass from a parent to its children. CSS was not the first style-sheet idea, but its collaboration with HTML and browser standards made it foundational. The demo uses modern CSS to make that separation visible.

1995 · JavaScript

A click becomes a conversation.

May 1995: initial prototype. 1997: the first ECMAScript standard.

The browser can run your logic.

JavaScript gives a page behavior. A click can update a value, validate input or reveal an answer immediately. The browser becomes a place where programs run, right beside the content.

Eich built the first prototype in ten days; the language then evolved through years of work by many people. JavaScript is distinct from Java. Events connect a user action to a function, and browser APIs let that function change what the visitor sees. The example here uses modern JavaScript syntax.

1998 · DOM

Meet the tree behind the page.

October 1998: DOM Level 1 Recommendation. Browser-specific DOMs existed earlier.

Find a node. Change the experience.

The Document Object Model exposes a document as objects arranged in a tree. Scripts can inspect, create, edit and remove nodes through a shared interface.

The DOM is a browser API, not part of the JavaScript language itself. HTML is parsed into a document tree; scripts then manipulate that tree. A common model helped developers move beyond incompatible browser-specific approaches. Modern frameworks still ultimately update what a browser displays through these underlying capabilities.

W3C DOM Working Group — A collaborative browser standard

  • Read DOM Level 1 — W3C · Recommendation, 1 October 1998

2005 · AJAX

Update a little. Keep everything else.

1999: early XMLHttpRequest in IE. 2005: the AJAX name popularizes the pattern.

The page stays. The data changes.

AJAX combines scripting, background HTTP requests and targeted DOM updates. A map can load another area, or an inbox can fetch new messages, without rebuilding the entire page.

AJAX was a way to combine existing capabilities, not a new language or a single invention. The X stands for XML, but responses need not use XML; JSON is common today. Modern fetch() continues the same basic idea. The demo compares update scope with local data and a simulated delay, not a network-speed benchmark.

Jesse James Garrett · browser teams — Garrett named the approach; the underlying work predates the name

2008–09 · V8 / Node

Small scripts. Serious applications.

2008: V8 ships with Chrome. 2009: Node.js is introduced.

JavaScript grows beyond the page.

V8 pushes JavaScript execution forward with native-code compilation and runtime optimization. In 2009, Node.js brings V8 together with server-side APIs and asynchronous I/O.

V8 did not invent just-in-time compilation, and Node.js was not the first server-side JavaScript system. Their impact was in performance, architecture and the ecosystem they enabled. Asynchronous I/O lets a runtime handle other work while waiting for a network or file operation. CPU-heavy JavaScript can still block the event loop.

2010 · Responsive

One Web. Every screen.

May 2010: the original Responsive Web Design essay.

A layout that listens to its surroundings.

Responsive design brings fluid grids, flexible images and CSS media queries together. The same content can adapt to a phone, a tablet or a large display.

Marcotte brought these techniques together into a coherent approach; he did not invent all of the underlying CSS features. Responsive design also asks us to consider input methods, reading order and performance. Move the viewport control to see one real document reflow at different widths.

Ethan Marcotte — Named and articulated responsive web design

  • Read the original essay — Ethan Marcotte · A List Apart, 2010

2011–14 · Web platform

Real time. Real sound. A new dimension.

2011: WebSocket RFC and WebGL 1.0. 2014: HTML5 Recommendation.

Native capabilities replace many plug-ins.

WebSocket supports an ongoing two-way connection. WebGL brings GPU graphics into a canvas. HTML5 standardizes richer native media and application features. The browser becomes a capable home for apps.

These are related advances, not one technology released on one day. HTML5 features shipped before the 2014 Recommendation. WebSocket connects clients to a server; WebGL provides graphics APIs; HTML defines media and document features. Standards groups, browser vendors and many individual contributors made them interoperable.

IETF · Khronos · WHATWG & W3C — Including Ian Fette, Alexey Melnikov and HTML5 editor Ian Hickson

2012–14 · Frameworks

Small pieces. A living whole.

2012: AngularJS 1.0. 2013: React is open-sourced. 2014: Vue is released.

Components + state + a way to grow.

AJAX keeps a page alive. But a growing app has dozens of things to keep in sync: buttons, forms, lists and navigation. Frameworks and UI libraries give those pieces structure. Describe the interface around its data, then let the system coordinate updates.

This chapter follows a change in how applications are built, rather than a new browser capability. Earlier libraries and frameworks had already tackled browser differences and application structure; these three did not invent components or declarative programming. AngularJS, originally created by Miško Hevery and Adam Abrons, reached 1.0 in June 2012 after earlier development. It used templates, data binding and dependency injection. Angular 2, released in 2016, was a major rewrite, not simply a new name for AngularJS. Jordan Walke created React at Facebook; its 2013 open-source release helped popularize composing interfaces from components and describing views from state. React is a UI library, often combined with other tools or an application framework. Evan You released Vue in 2014, offering reactive templates and a progressively adoptable approach. Their mechanisms differ, and none replaces HTML, CSS, JavaScript or the DOM. The practical gain is a more manageable growing application; the costs include dependencies, tooling and a learning curve. A simple document may need none of them. The interactive example demonstrates shared state using React, not a performance comparison between the three.

2015 · Offline / PWA

The network leaves. The app can stay.

2015: the PWA concept is named and promoted, as early service worker support develops.

Service workers + web app manifests.

A service worker can serve deliberately cached responses when the network is gone. A web app manifest gives an app its name, icons and launch preferences. Progressive Web Apps bring these capabilities together into a web experience you can install and return to.

PWA means Progressive Web App. It describes an application model built from existing and evolving web capabilities, not a new programming language or one API. Berriman and Russell helped name and articulate the idea in 2015. HTTPS, responsive design, a web app manifest and an intentional service-worker/cache strategy can let an experience move from a tab to a home-screen icon and keep useful content available offline. Installation does not itself provide offline behavior, and browser/platform support varies. Service workers cannot directly edit the DOM. The preview on this page simulates installation and caching; it does not install this history site.

2017 · WebAssembly

More languages. One open platform.

2017: the initial version reaches major browsers. 2019: W3C Recommendation.

Compile to a portable binary format.

WebAssembly provides a compact instruction format designed for efficient execution. Code from languages such as C, C++ and Rust can join JavaScript in browser applications.

WebAssembly complements JavaScript rather than replacing HTML, CSS or browser APIs. It runs within a sandbox and communicates through defined interfaces. Useful workloads include games, audio processing, CAD and scientific computing. Performance depends on the task; compiling to Wasm is not a universal speed-up.

2023 · WebGPU

Thousands of tasks. Working together.

2023: Chrome 113 begins shipping WebGPU on supported platforms.

Modern graphics. General-purpose GPU compute.

WebGPU exposes modern GPU capabilities for rendering and computation. It opens new possibilities for large simulations, creative tools and machine-learning workloads inside the browser.

This date marks a browser shipping milestone, not the moment every browser or device supported WebGPU. Compute shaders can apply the same operation to many independent data items. The right workload and data-transfer costs matter. The demonstration illustrates parallel work; it does not claim a measured speed advantage.

W3C GPU for the Web Community Group — A collaborative effort across browser and GPU teams
